# Of the Chart and of Sleep

*How far there is to go, and how to cross it.*

## Reading the chart

The chart on the cabin table shows the whole world. Land is green and brown, shallows are pale, and deep water is dark. Every port is marked with its name, and the one you are bound for has a **gold ring**.

- **North** is at the top.
- The **grid** lines are fifty kilometres apart, and every second line is marked with its number. The **scale bar** in the corner is a hundred kilometres long. Lay it against the distance you want.
- Your ship is the small **yellow arrow**, pointing the way she heads.
- Round the arrow is a **ring**. The longer you have been away from the last port, the **wider the ring** grows, for no master is ever quite sure where he is. Out of sight of land, trust the ring and not the point.
- The dashed gold line is a safe road to the port. It goes round the land.

## Knots and kilometres

The log gives your speed in **knots**. The chart is in **kilometres**. One knot is **1.852 kilometres in an hour**, so:

**kilometres per hour = knots × 1.852**

**distance in kilometres = knots × 1.852 × hours**

- 3 knots: 5.6 kilometres an hour
- 5 knots: 9.3 kilometres an hour
- 6 knots: 11.1 kilometres an hour
- 8 knots: 14.8 kilometres an hour
- 10 knots: 18.5 kilometres an hour

A ship making **6 knots** goes **11.1 km** in an hour, and **222 km** in twenty hours.

## How many hours?

Read the **distance** off the chart, take your **speed** from the log, and divide:

**hours = distance ÷ (knots × 1.852)**

A port **150 km** away, at **5 knots** (9.3 km an hour), is about **16 hours** off.

## Sleep

Click the bed. You are asked how many hours. Type a number and press Enter, or press Esc to get up again.

While you sleep the ship **keeps her heading and her speed** at the moment you lay down.

- Before you sleep, **hold your course** and be sure the sails are set and drawing. A ship lying idle, or turned the wrong way, will carry you nowhere or somewhere you do not want to be.
- You **wake early** at a mark on the way, when a port is close, when land is ahead, or at the edge of the chart. You will not run aground in your sleep.
- Then look at the chart again. The arrow will have moved, and the ring will be wider.

## Marks on the way

The gold **diamond** on the horizon is the next mark on your road, with its distance beneath. When you wake at one, the diamond moves on to the next. When it shows the port, you are nearly there.

# Of the Compass and the Stars

*How a master knows where he is when there is nothing to see.*

Out of sight of land there is no mark to steer by, and the sea looks the same in every direction. A master finds his place by **reckoning**, and by the stars when he can.

## Dead reckoning

Three things are needed, and the ship gives them all:

1. **The course**, from the compass in the binnacle.
2. **The speed**, from the log and line (see *Of the Log and Line*).
3. **The time** sailed on that course.

Speed multiplied by time gives the distance run. Lay it off along the course from where you started and you have your place. A ship that makes **5 knots** for **3 hours** has gone **15 nautical miles**, which is **28 kilometres** on the chart (a knot is 1.852 km an hour; see *Of the Chart and of Sleep*).

Mark the new place on the chart in the cabin. Do it often, and every time the course or the speed changes.

## Why you can never be sure

The reckoning is never exact. The log gives the speed through the **water**, and a current may be carrying ship and water together, which the log will never show. The compass card may be a degree or two out. Wind and sea push the ship off her course between your readings, and a hasty glass gives a false speed.

On the chart the **ring** about your ship shows this. The longer you are away from the last port, the wider it grows. A few hours out it is small. After days on open water it may be larger than the island you look for.

## The stars

On a clear night the stars do not drift. A master who can find his latitude by them has a fixed place to start from, and the ring of doubt shrinks to nothing. This is the **hard** way and asks more of the navigator.

## Hiring a pilot

A sailor who knows these waters can be hired in a port tavern and will come aboard with you. Ask him, and he will point toward the port you seek, and tell you how far it lies. He will not sail the ship for you, and he can be wrong.

# Of Crew and Hammocks

*How many hands a ship wants, and where she puts them.*

## Hands

A ship sails with fewer men than she needs and does it badly. The brig can be sailed by a **single man** if he works every line himself, but each sail he sets takes him time, for he must walk from rope to rope. A crew of **eight to ten** sails her well. She will carry **twelve** at the most, and every ship has a smallest crew she can be trusted to. For the brig it is **five**.

More hands also work faster. One man raises one sail at a time. A larger crew raises several at once.

## Where they sleep

Each sailor has a **hammock**, and the hammocks are slung in sets of three between posts. The number of hammocks aboard is the number of sailors she can carry. The brig has room for only so many sets, and more hammocks than she needs would leave no room for cargo.

A hammock takes up space that cargo would otherwise have. **A ship with a small crew carries more cargo.** A ship with a large crew carries less, but sails better and is harder to board.

The hammocks swing a little as the ship moves. This is as it should be.

## What they eat

Every man eats. **More men need more provisions**, and a ship that sets out with too few will have a hungry crew within days. Plan the stores for the length of the voyage and a little more.

## When a prize is taken

A ship you have taken is not sailed home by you. Put a **prize crew** aboard her, and she follows. A prize needs at least her own minimum crew. Without them she will not stay with you, and you will have gained nothing by taking her.

# Of Docking and Mooring

*How a ship is brought to a pier without breaking her or it.*

## The berth

Each pier has berths marked out for the ships it can take, and each berth has a size. A small pier will not take a large ship. A berth shows itself as a **glowing rectangle on the water** as you come near. It is cut to the size of the ship that is meant to lie there.

## Coming in

1. **Slow down.** A ship that comes in too fast cannot be moored, and will strike the pier. The berth will tell you the speed is too great.
2. **Line her up** with the berth. The pier lies on the **port** side as you come in. The berth has a heading of its own, and the ship must lie close to it.
3. **Bring the whole hull inside the rectangle.** If the light is red, she is not yet in, or is too fast, or is crooked. When she is in, slow enough and straight, it turns **green**.
4. **Give the order to put the lines ashore.** The ship is then drawn in against the fenders by the lines to the bollards, and held. After a moment the **gangway** is run out to the pier.

You cannot walk off the pier side until the gangway is out.

## Casting off

Give the order again to **cast off**. The lines are let go and the ship drifts off the pier. You cannot cast off while a man is standing on the gangway.

## Dangers

- **Shoal water.** The keel reaches more than two metres below the water. If it touches the bottom the ship slows and is pushed back toward deeper water. The waves count, so a trough can ground you where a crest would not. Watch the water under the keel when you are near land.
- **The pier.** If the hull strikes it, the ship is stopped and thrown back, and the harder you hit, the worse it is.
- **The wind** will push a ship off her line as she nears the pier. Come in slowly enough to correct for it.

# Of the Log and Line

*How a master learns the speed of his ship.*

A ship has no milestones. The wind can be strong and the ship slow, or the wind fair and gentle and the ship quick, and a man cannot tell by looking at the sea. The only honest way is to measure the ship against the water, and this is done with the log.

## What you will need

- **The line**: a coil of rope lies on the poop deck by the stern rail. It runs up and over the rail and down the outside of the stern, to the log chip in the water. First comes a length of plain line, called the *stray line*. Then a **red block**, the mark. After the mark, a plain **wooden block** is seized to the line at every fixed distance.
- **The glass**: the sand glass that stands on the stern rail beside the line. It runs for **twenty-eight seconds**.

## How it is done

1. **Heave the log.** Take hold of the coil, and the line pays out over the rail. The chip stays where it is in the water while the ship sails on, so the line runs out at the speed of the ship. Heave it with the ship under way. A ship standing still pulls out no line at all.
2. **Let the stray line run.** The plain line goes first. It carries the chip clear of the ship's wake, where the water is still. Do not start counting yet.
3. **Watch for the red block.** When it goes over the rail, **turn the glass**, and no sooner or later.
4. **Count the wooden blocks** as they go over the rail, until the glass is out.
5. When the last sand falls the line is **held fast**. The blocks you counted are all the ship has made.

If you walk away from the coil, or take hold of it again, the line is hauled in. To take another reading, heave it again.

## What it tells you

The blocks are spaced to fit the glass, so **every block that goes over the rail is one knot of speed.** Count five, and the ship is making five knots. A faster ship runs out more line in the same twenty-eight seconds.

A knot is a measure of speed, and it is the one the whole trade is reckoned in. One knot is one nautical mile in the hour, which is **1.852 kilometres in the hour**. Once you know your speed, set it against the time you have sailed and you have the distance you have made. With your heading, that puts you on the chart.

## Cautions

- **Turn the glass at the red block, not before it and not after.** A glass turned early gives too many blocks, and one turned late gives too few.
- A hasty count, a slack line, or a chip that drags along with the ship will all tell you a speed that is not true. Heave the log once more and compare the two.
- The log gives the ship's speed **through the water**. It will not tell you of a current that carries ship and water together. For that you want the stars, the coast, or a lead line.

---

### Notes for development (not shown to the player)

- The game never states a speed number for the log line; it is read off the blocks (see `scripts/ship_log_line.gd`).
- Real figures kept: block spacing 14.4 m (47 ft 3 in), glass 28 s, stray line about 12 fathoms (about 22 m) before the mark.
- The line is drawn running out slowly (0.3 m of model line per real 14.4 m) so a block goes over the rail in the same time it would at sea. The player counts timing, not the speed of the rope.
- Count rule: blocks sit half a spacing off the mark, so a count equals the speed rounded to the nearest knot.
- Controls: click the coil to heave the log (click again, or walk away, to haul it in); click the glass to turn it. The rope's path is the LogLine_P0 to P4 markers in the brig.

# Your Orders

*Read this first.*

The owners have given you this ship and one task. **Carry her from the port where she lies to the port ringed in gold on the chart in the cabin.** Everything you need is in the books on this shelf.

## The passage

1. **Study the chart** on the table in the cabin. Click it and it fills your sight. The gold ring is your destination. Out on the water, a **gold diamond** on the horizon, with a distance under it, shows the way and how far there is to go.
2. **Cast off** from the pier.
3. **Set the sails.** Their lines hang from pins at the rails by the masts. Ease a line out and the sail drops and sets. Turn the yards with the braces until the sails fill.
4. **Steer** with the wheel, by the compass in front of it, toward the diamond.
5. **Learn your speed** with the log and line: click the coil of rope on the poop deck by the stern rail, and count the blocks that go over the rail while the sand glass beside it runs.
6. **Sleep through the long hours.** Click the bed, say how many, and the ship holds her heading and speed. You wake early at a mark, a port, land, or the edge of the chart. Work out the hours from your speed and the distance on the chart.
7. **Come in slowly** when the port is close. Line her up with the berth and put the lines ashore.

## What your hands can do

Walk with **W A S D**, run with **Shift**, jump with **Space**, look with the mouse. **Esc** frees the mouse.

**Left click works the ship.** Anything you can use is outlined in white when you look at it: the wheel, the ropes, the pump handle, the chart, the bed, the bookshelf, the coil of log line and its sand glass. Click it, or hold the button for the wheel, the ropes and the pump.

At the wheel the keys you may use are shown at the foot of the screen: **Q** the wheel amidships, **Z** hold the course, and **V** the compass. At the pier, **E** puts the lines ashore, and **E** again casts off.

## Aloft

To see farther, climb to the **lookout barrel** on the main mast. Go to the rope ladder (the shrouds) at the side of the main mast, step up to it, and climb with **W**, with **S** to come down. Near the top of the ropes you are drawn over to the ladder up the mast, and near the top of that you go up through the hatch into the barrel. In the barrel you stand and look about. Press any key that moves you (**W A S D** or **Space**) and you are put back on the ladder to climb down.

## The other books

- *Of Sails and the Wind* and *Of the Wheel and the Course*: how to make her go, and steer.
- *Of the Log and Line* and *Of the Chart and of Sleep*: how fast, how far, and how long.
- *Of Docking and Mooring*: how to arrive.
- *Of the Compass and the Stars*, *Of Weight and Sinking* and *Of Crew and Hammocks*: the rest of the trade.

# Of Sails and the Wind

*How a ship is made to go, and how she is made to stop.*

A ship goes by the wind and by nothing else. The whole art is to set the cloth so that the wind pushes her where you wish to go, and to take the cloth in again when it does her harm.

## The lines

Every sail has a line hanging from a **belaying pin** on a rail beside its mast. The jib and the staysail, and the sails of the foremast, are worked at the rail abaft the foremast. The sails of the mainmast and the spanker are worked at the rail abaft the mainmast.

Take hold of the end of a line and **haul it down**: the sail is gathered up and furled. A square sail goes halfway first, which is called **reefed**, and then all the way. **Ease the line upward** and the sail drops and sets. Let go, and the pin holds whatever you have done.

A strong wind makes the cloth heavy. Hauling takes more work the harder it blows.

## The braces

The square sails hang from yards that swing like gates. Two **braces** on each mast, one on the port bulwark and one on the starboard, turn the yards.

- Haul the port brace and the port end of the yards swings aft. Haul the starboard brace and it goes the other way.
- A sail with the wind coming at it from the side, and filled at a slant, pulls the ship along.
- A sail turned square to the wind has no push in it and only drags. A sail turned too sharp, or pointed too close to the wind, shakes and gives nothing.
- A sail with the wind on its **front** is said to be **aback**, and it pushes the ship **astern**.

The fore-and-aft sails, the jib, the staysail and the spanker, are trimmed by the crew, so a ship with no hands in her will not have these set well.

## Reading the wind

The pennant on its staff by the wheel shows the wind **as the ship feels it**. That is not the same as the wind blowing over the sea. A ship that is moving makes a wind of her own, and the two are added together, so the faster you go the further ahead the wind appears to come.

A pennant hanging limp means a light air. When it flies level, there is a good breeze.

## Where the wind should be

How fast she goes depends on where the wind is **relative to the ship**. Read it from the pennant, and from the sails. These are rough speeds for a brig in a fresh breeze with all her proper sail set:

- **Wind from dead ahead, or within about forty-five degrees of it:** she cannot sail into it. The sails shake and give nothing.
- **Close to the wind**, about fifty to sixty degrees off the bow: slow, five knots or so, and she leans far over.
- **Wind abeam, from the side:** a good, steady seven or eight knots.
- **Wind on the quarter, from behind and to one side:** her best, eight to ten knots.
- **Wind from dead astern:** seven or eight knots, and less than you would hope, for the forward sails are becalmed behind the others.

She will not go much over **ten knots** whatever the wind does. In a **gale** (thirty knots and more), take in the topgallants and reef the topsails and the courses first, or she will be driven too hard and leaned too far.

To go somewhere the wind will not let you, sail across it first and then across it the other way, bringing her round, so that the wind falls on one side and then the other, working toward the place a little at a time.

## What to expect

- A ship under sail leans over. The taller her sails, the more she leans.
- She also slides a little sideways through the water, which is called **leeway**, and the keel resists this better the faster she goes.
- She wants to turn up into the wind by herself, which is called **weather helm**, and the rudder has to hold her against it.
- A brig will not go much faster than ten knots, however hard it blows.
- With the wind straight from astern, the sails in front sit in the lee of those behind them and take less wind.

# Of Weight and Sinking

*Why a ship that carries too much does not carry it far.*

## Everything weighs something

The ship floats because the water she pushes aside weighs as much as she does. Whatever is put aboard makes her heavier, sits her lower in the water, and makes her slower. That is true of cargo and of men, of the provisions and of the guns.

The **cannon** are the heaviest things aboard that are not cargo. A ship that sends her guns ashore sits higher and sails faster. A master who has no wish to fight may think this a good bargain. One who meets a pirate will not.

## The waterline

Look at the rails. If the water is a long way below them, all is well. As the ship is loaded, the sea comes nearer. If the **waterline stays above the rails** for more than a few moments, the sea comes aboard faster than it can run out, and the ship is lost.

- Do not load a ship until her rails are almost awash and then take her out into a heavy sea.
- A load that would sink her in a swell may be carried safely in a calm. Weigh the weather as well as the cargo.
- Cargo too heavy to carry by hand is loaded by the **harbour crane**. Look to the weight before it is swung aboard, not after.

## Leaks

A ship that strikes a rock, or is struck by shot, will let in water. The water collects in the hold and adds its own weight to the ship, and a heavier ship sits lower still.

- The **pumps** drive water out of the hold. Take hold of the **pump handle** (it is outlined when you look at it) and keep your hold: the handle works up and down under your hands, and the pumps run for as long as you hold on. Let go and they stop. They work slowly, and a hole that is large will beat them.
- A hole can be **plugged**, and this should be done before anything else.

## What to do

Know what your ship will bear. Keep the stores, the crew and the guns in proportion. Keep the pumps in order. If the rails are going under, throw the cargo over the side before the ship is lost, for the cargo can be bought again.

# Of the Wheel and the Course

*How a ship is steered, and kept steering.*

## The wheel

The wheel turns the rudder, and the rudder turns the ship. Take hold of the rim at any spot and move your hand the way the rim moves under it. Turning the wheel to the right, as you stand behind it, puts the rudder over so that the ship turns to **starboard**. Turning it to the left sends her to **port**.

Hold the wheel and your eyes stay where they are. Let go and you may look about again.

## Way on

A rudder does nothing until water runs past it. A ship lying still, or nearly so, will not answer her wheel at all. She must have **way on**, and the faster she goes the quicker she turns. Even so she is slow to begin and slow to stop, so ease the wheel back before she has swung as far as you want.

## Amidships and holding a course

When the wheel is straight, the rudder is **amidships**. You can bring the wheel back to this without your hand and let her run.

You can also ask a steady hand to **hold the course** you are on. The wheel then moves of itself, a little at a time, as a good helmsman's would, to keep her head where it is. The course stays held even after you walk away, to haul a line or look at the chart. It is let go if you take the wheel yourself, or ask for it.

The words for these orders are shown at the foot of your sight whenever your hand is on the wheel.

## The compass

Before you hold a course, know it. The compass stands in the binnacle just ahead of the wheel. The card inside it keeps its north, and the ship turns round it. The **red mark** on the rim is fixed to the ship and points at her bow, so the number under the mark is the way she is heading.

A bearing is given in degrees from north, going round with the sun: east is ninety, south one hundred and eighty, west two hundred and seventy.

## Cautions

- A ship under sail pulls to windward by herself (**weather helm**). Expect to hold a little wheel against it.
- Heavy weather and a heavy sea will carry her off her course. A held course is a good servant and a poor master. Look at the compass.
